questions.stem: In two identical squares of side length \(c+d\), the first square contains an inner tilted quadrilateral formed by joining points that divide each side in the ratio \(c:d\). The second square is divided into two smaller squares of sides \(c\) and \(d\), and two rectangles of dimensions \(c \times d\).

parts.stem: Prove that the tilted inner quadrilateral (formed by joining points that divide each side of the square in the ratio \(c:d\)) is a square.
parts.answer: Each side of the inner quadrilateral is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs \(c\) and \(d\), so every side has length \(\sqrt{c^2+d^2}\) (all sides equal). At each vertex, the two acute angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) of the adjoining triangles satisfy \(\alpha+\beta=90°\), so the interior angle is \(180°-(\alpha+\beta)=90°\) (all angles equal). Equal sides and right angles confirm it is a square.
parts.hint: Show (i) all four sides are equal in length, and (ii) all four interior angles are \(90°\).
parts.solution: Each side of the inner quadrilateral is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs \(c\) and \(d\), so every side has length \(\sqrt{c^2+d^2}\) (all sides equal). At each vertex, the two acute angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) of the adjoining triangles satisfy \(\alpha+\beta=90°\), so the interior angle is \(180°-(\alpha+\beta)=90°\) (all angles equal). Equal sides and right angles confirm it is a square.

steps.explain: Each side of the inner quadrilateral is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs \(c\) and \(d\).
This is true for all four corner triangles (by the symmetry of the construction), so all four sides of the inner quadrilateral are equal.
At each vertex of the inner quadrilateral, let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be the two acute angles of the adjoining right-angled triangles. Since each triangle is right-angled, \(\alpha+\beta=90°\).
The straight angle along the outer square's side is \(180°\), so the interior angle of the inner quadrilateral is \(180°-(\alpha+\beta)\).
All four sides are equal and all four angles are \(90°\), so the inner quadrilateral is a square.

parts.stem: Let \(a\) be the side length of the tilted inner square (from part a). The two large squares shown are both \((c+d)\times(c+d)\), so their areas are equal. steps.explain: Its area, found this second way, is:
Both squares have the same side length \(c+d\), so their areas are equal. Equate the two expressions.
Cancel \(2cd\) from both sides to obtain Pythagoras' theorem.

questions.hint: Use Pythagoras' theorem $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ to write expressions for the areas.

steps.explain: a) Show all four sides of the inner quadrilateral are equal.
steps.work: \text{Each side is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs } c \text{ and } d. \text{ Therefore, length of each side } = \sqrt{c^2 + d^2}.

steps.explain: Show all four angles of the inner quadrilateral are 90 degrees.
steps.work: \text{Let the two acute angles of each corner right-angled triangle be } \alpha \text{ and } \beta. \text{ Since it is a right-angled triangle, } \alpha + \beta = 90^\circ. \text{ The straight line angle is } 180^\circ. \text{ The angle at the vertex is } 180^\circ - (\alpha + \beta) = 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ.

steps.explain: b) Set up area equation for the first square.
steps.work: \text{Area of first square} = (c+d)^2 = c^2 + 2cd + d^2. \text{ It also equals } 4 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}cd\right) + a^2 = 2cd + a^2.

steps.explain: Equate the areas of the two representations to prove Pythagoras' theorem.
steps.work: 2cd + a^2 = c^2 + 2cd + d^2 \Rightarrow a^2 = c^2 + d^2. \text{ This proves Pythagoras' theorem.}

questions.stem: Determine whether or not the triangle with the side lengths 12, 35, 37 is right-angled.
questions.hint: Check if the squares of the two smaller sides sum to the square of the longest side: \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).
questions.solution: The correct answer is Yes, it is right-angled.

steps.explain: Identify the three sides in ascending order: $a = 12$, $b = 35$, and the longest side (potential hypotenuse) $c = 37$.
Sum the squares of the two smaller sides: \(a^2 + b^2\).
Compare this sum with the square of the longest side (\(c^2 = 1369\)).
steps.work: \text{Since } a^2 + b^2 = c^2 \text{ (1369 = 1369), it forms a right-angled triangle (Yes).}

Multiply the outer coefficient into the first term: $3 \times 5 = 15$.
Collect the like surds (both are $\sqrt{3}$ terms): $15+5=20$. The $\sqrt{5}$ term has no like term to combine with.
